title: Newtown: Settlement, War and Reserved Native Rights
summary: Newtown was a colonial town in western Queens, centered near present-day Elmhurst. English settlers obtained Dutch government grants, then further Native agreements under English rule. Named officials and settlers expanded claims over land where Native rights had remained reserved.

why_this_matters: Colonial grants and Native land agreements were different acts. Their sequence shows how settlement expanded, while reserved rights and continuing communities challenge a story of simple disappearance.

history_title: How control of the land changed
history_content:
Where is Newtown, and whose colony was it?

Newtown was a colonial town in western Queens, New York City; its village center became part of present-day Elmhurst. The larger town stretched toward the East River and Flushing Creek. Mespat and Middleburgh were earlier settlement names in this district, not separate European countries. English settlers established communities here within New Netherland, the colony governed by the Dutch West India Company. English origin and Dutch colonial rule therefore appear together in this history. Newtown historical background, pp. 3–4

A homeland before Newtown

The creeks, shorelines and wooded hills of western Queens were Native places before colonists called this district Mespat, Middleburgh or Newtown. A sequence of colonial grants and agreements gradually changed who could settle, cultivate and claim these lands. The documents do not describe one moment when an entire people surrendered its homeland. They also record rights that Native proprietors continued to hold after settlers arrived. The Annals of Newtown

A colonial grant and a war

In 1642, Willem Kieft, the Dutch director of New Netherland, granted a large tract to Reverend Francis Doughty and a group of settlers from New England. Kieft represented the colonial government; Doughty and his associates were the recipients who intended to settle it. This was a colonial government's grant, not itself a deed from Native owners. The following year, war precipitated by Kieft's actions reached the settlement at Mespat. Native attackers destroyed the settlement and its surviving settlers fled to New Amsterdam. In 1652, English Calvinist settlers from New England obtained permission from Dutch director Peter Stuyvesant to establish Middleburgh near today’s Queens Boulevard and Grand Avenue in Elmhurst. Jonathan Fish and Robert Coe were among these settlers. The history of the land therefore includes warfare and competing authorities before the later instruments that colonists used to secure title. Newtown Playground: general historical background

Native rights remained after an earlier agreement

The July 9, 1666 deed transcribed by James Riker names Rowerowestco and Pomwaukon and recites an earlier agreement from 1656. The earlier arrangement had not given colonists unrestricted use of every part of the tract: Native hunting privileges remained in southern uplands, while settlers had specified mowing, grazing and timber rights. The record also restricted the Native proprietors from selling their reserved privileges to anyone except Newtown's inhabitants. By 1666, settlers were occupying land where those privileges remained. Richard Betts, acting for Newtown’s settlers, obtained Governor Richard Nicolls’s permission to negotiate a further purchase. Nicolls represented England’s new colonial government after English forces took New Netherland in 1664. The Native parties named in the resulting instrument were Rowerowestco and Pomwaukon. Nicolls administration: New York State Archives documents The Annals of Newtown

The next deed and the patent

The 1666 instrument recorded an additional payment and a release of the reserved privileges. The following March, English governor Richard Nicolls issued a patent naming Richard Betts, Thomas Lawrence, John Coe, John Burroughes, Ralph Hunt, Daniel Whitehead and Burger Joost, on behalf of themselves and their associates. A patent was a colonial government’s formal grant or confirmation of a land claim. It used Flushing Creek, the Sound, Mespat waterways and the hills toward Jamaica to describe the town claim. Its language covered land already purchased and land that might be purchased afterward: the broad patent was not evidence that every part had already been transferred by Native owners. Deeds, settlement and colonial government worked together to turn overlapping relationships to land into inheritable town and private claims. The Annals of Newtown

Reading the record without erasing people

These documents are evidence of particular claims, promises and restrictions. They cannot establish that every Native person consented or that Native relationships with the place ended. Riker's surrounding nineteenth-century account assumes Native disappearance; that interpretation is not adopted here. The map should show the approximate landscape of the named claim, while the article preserves the distinction between a colonial patent and the lives and rights of its Native inhabitants. The Annals of Newtown

The shoreline changed after the deeds

The modern waterfront is not the shoreline described in the colonial records. New York City’s environmental history of Flushing Bay explains that LaGuardia Airport expanded by filling wetlands, followed by runway extensions into the surrounding bays. A place shown as dry land on today’s map may therefore have been water or marsh when the earlier agreements were made. This later transformation belongs in the land story, but it is not evidence of a Native sale of the airport’s modern footprint. NYC DEP, Flushing Bay plan, section 2.1, p. 2-1

Living communities in Queens

The wider Queens story continues through Matinecock descendants and their cultural work. Flushing Town Hall’s 2018 program brought named descendants together to discuss history, protocols and relationships with local institutions. This contemporary connection does not establish an otherwise uncertain tribal identification for each seventeenth-century signatory. Honoring the First People of Queens

Continue with Matinecock Ancestral Land and Matinecock Way.
whereintheworld_content:
This is a regional reading area for Newtown in western Queens, including today’s Elmhurst, Astoria and the Bowery Bay–LaGuardia waterfront. Its inland outline uses H. F. Walling’s 1859 town geography; the northern coastal edge includes the modern Queens shoreline so that changes to the waterfront can be understood in the same account. It is not the footprint of a single Native deed, a seventeenth-century shoreline or proof that Native rights ended. The historical map alignment differs by up to about 500 metres, and the coast was later altered by filling and construction. The named creeks and hills in the historical instruments remain important evidence, but this display is not a parcel survey. The separate Seller Neck meadow interest mentioned in the Newtown patent is not included.

Walling’s 1859 map; Modern Queens coastline

At the Bushwick–Ridgewood and Highland Park edge, this regional reading area overlaps the neighboring Brooklyn history. The historical map alignment is approximate; the overlap connects relevant histories without claiming a recovered colonial boundary. It does not represent an additional Native sale. Read the neighboring Brooklyn history

The regional reading area continues to today's Hunters Point and Blissville waterfronts. The modern coast helps locate this history but is not a seventeenth-century deed line. EPA describes how industrial and government activity filled wetlands, reshaped Newtown Creek and reinforced its banks; the city's Hunters Point park account also documents later shoreline construction. These changes make the present water's edge an unreliable substitute for the creeks and shores named in colonial documents. The outline connects the places to the existing Native land-rights history; it does not record an additional Native sale.
